title: weight-loading-and-hot-swap-spec-draft
body:
Purpose
This draft specifies how Redwood's serving runtime should manage model weights on disk and in memory to minimize latency and cost while enabling safe, fast model variant swaps (hot swap). It focuses on three orthogonal mechanisms: lazy/streaming load, memory-mapped (mmap) backing for large weights, and an atomic hot-swap path for model version rollouts or emergency fallback.

Context & goals
- Workloads: multi-tenant hosted API, dedicated GPU pools, and private deployments with constrained host memory.
- Constraints: GPUs with limited VRAM, varied container memory limits, and ephemeral nodes.
- Primary goals: ensure predictable cold-start latency, reduce peak host memory use, permit safe, low-latency model swaps, and maintain reproducible behavior across hosted/dedicated/private environments.

Non-goals
- This doc does not prescribe kernel-level operator implementations (attention, matmul kernels). It focuses on file/OS-level and runtime orchestration for weight residency and transitions.

Key concepts and terminology
- Resident weight: weight tensor memory present in process address space (CPU or GPU).
- Backing store: on-disk artifact (safetensors, pt, or custom format) used as canonical source for weights.
- Mmap-backed read-only mapping: OS-level memory mapping of weight file pages that act as a cold reservoir for weight pages that can be faulted into RAM on access.
- Lazy load: incremental transfer of weights from backing store (via mmap/prefetch/streaming) to device or GPU staging buffer on first access or on policy-based prefetch.
- Hot swap: atomic replacement of an in-memory model graph+weights with another model artifact/version without dropping in-flight requests beyond a bounded safe window.
- Ejection/eviction: mechanism to release resident weight pages under memory pressure following policy.

Supported on-disk formats
- Primary supported formats: safetensors (preferred), torch .pt (legacy), and raw contiguous binary blobs produced by model-conversion pipelines.
- Safetensors: preferred because of deterministic layout and safe zero-copy mapping semantics. Recommendation: convert and publish all production-serving artifacts as safetensors with consistent naming and version manifests.

Design overview
1) Start-up & cold load policy
- Check manifest: on process model load, read a manifest that includes model id, version, file path, format, quantization metadata, and a per-layer loading_priority integer.
- If backing store is local (dedicated/private) and is safetensors: create an mmap read-only mapping for the whole weight file to minimize peak working memory; do not fault-in pages until accessed.
- If backing store remote (hosted S3 / network FS): policy depends on network characteristics: for high-throughput nodes, prefetch header + layer offsets and enable streaming reads into a staging area; for lower-bandwidth nodes, perform small-chunk streaming on first access.
- If model size <= gpu-resident-threshold (config, e.g., 6GB for small GPU configs) and GPU memory is available, optionally eagerly upload full weights to GPU to optimize inference latency for always-hot models. This is a config knob per deployment.

2) Lazy loading and per-layer strategy
- Per-layer metadata: manifest defines each tensor with offset, size, dtype, quantization type, and loading_priority. Runtimes should honor loading_priority for prefetching.
- Access path: when a layer is first invoked, the weight loading subsystem attempts to ensure the tensor is resident on the target device. For mmap-backed files, this usually means reading the page(s) or invoking madvise+/posix_fadvise-driven prefetch. For non-mmap remote files, stream the layer into a CPU buffer then transfer to GPU.
- Prefetch heuristics: predictability drives UX. Default heuristic: prefetch the first N layers (N configurable) and layers with high loading_priority; for chat-style generation, prefetch attention + normalization weights early.

3) Memory-mapping and shared mmaps across workers
- Mmap semantics: open file with O_RDONLY and map PROT_READ. For safetensors, layout ensures tensors are contiguous and page-aligned. Use MAP_SHARED where possible so kernel can deduplicate pages across processes on the same host.
- Shared mmap pool: when multiple worker processes on same host use same file path and version, they should share the same open FD via a local mmapping manager (unix domain socket broker or coord service) to maximize page cache sharing.
- File descriptor lifecycle: FD kept open for lifetime of model usage; close only after final eviction. This allows the OS page cache to hold pages.

4) Device transfer and staging buffers
- Staged upload: transfers to GPU should use preallocated pinned CPU staging buffers to maximize PCIe/NVLink throughput. For large weights and quantized tensors, use chunked async copy streams to overlap compute and copy.
- Alignment: ensure tensor chunks are aligned to page boundaries to avoid extra page faults. Where necessary, copy into aligned staging buffers before async transfer.

5) Quantized/packed weights and zero-copy paths
- Where quantization permits (e.g., int8 with specific layout), support zero-copy mapping of packed weights into inference kernels that can read directly from mmap pages. If hardware requires unpacked layout, implement a fast in-place unpack during the first load and keep unpacked version in device memory and optionally cache decompressed CPU copy when eviction policies suggest reloading.

6) Hot-swap semantics and atomicity
- Goal: swap model A -> model B for new connections with minimal disruption to in-flight queries.
- Model handle versioning: runtime exposes an opaque model handle (GUID + version). Worker threads hold a pointer to the current model handle. Hot swap is a three-phase process: prepare, drain, commit.
  - Prepare: load backing artifacts for B (mmap, prefetch per policy, warm some hot layers according to loading_priority). Keep B in a staging state not visible to request path.
  - Drain: allow in-flight requests using A to finish. Track active requests with lightweight refcounts on the model handle. New requests after prepare are routed to B only after commit. Option: a brief forwarding window where new requests can be served by A or B depending on rollout policy (canary percentage).
  - Commit: atomically swap the worker-level pointer to B. Decrement reference to A; when refcount reaches zero, begin eviction of A (see eviction).
- Atomic pointer swap must be lockless for low latency: use standard atomic exchange for pointer-sized handle. Ensure memory barriers where required on platforms we support.

7) Eviction and reclamation policy
- Two-tier memory accounting: GPU-resident and CPU-resident. Both tracked per-model-version and per-layer.
- Eviction triggers: host OOM signals, memory reservation thresholds, explicit admin commands, or LRU-based reclamation under high concurrency.
- Safe eviction: only evict model A once refcount == 0 and no scheduled background tasks reference its tensors. Eviction may happen in steps: free transient CPU copies, then free GPU VRAM, finally close mmap FD if no longer needed.

8) Fallbacks and compatibility
- If hot swap fails (e.g., B cannot be prepared due to insufficient GPU memory), runtime supports fallback strategies in order: (1) scale to a lower-capacity variant (quantized or smaller model), (2) route to another region or capacity tier, (3) keep serving A and emit alert.
- Compatibility matrix: manifest must include required runtime features (e.g., 8-bit kernel availability, fused-op support). The load path should block or downgrade if kernels are incompatible with worker capabilities.

9) Security and file integrity
- Integrity verification: verify safetensors checksums from manifest before mapping. Use signature verification for enterprise/private deployments that require signed model artifacts.
- Permissions: mmap and file ownership checks to ensure worker is authorized to open backing store. For shared host mmaps, restrict shared broker to root or service account.

10) Observability and metrics
- Emit per-load metrics: cold-load latency (ms), bytes streamed from remote, page fault counts (if available), prefetch hit ratio, time-to-ready for staged model, number of hot swaps, failed hot swaps and reason codes.
- Trace events: prepare_start, prefetch_start(layer), prefetch_done(layer), commit, eviction_start, eviction_done. These should map to distributed tracing IDs in Redwood Console.

11) Testing and validation
- Unit tests: manifest parsing, mmap manager behavior (simulate shared mmaps), per-layer lazy load logic with artificial page fault counters.
- Integration tests: cold-start benchmarks for representative models (small: 1–3 GB, medium: 10–20 GB, large: >30 GB) on various node classes. Hot-swap correctness tests with concurrent requests verifying no request returns a mixed-model inference.
- Chaos tests: simulate OOM during prepare, corrupt backing store, and network blips during streaming load. Validate fallback behavior.

12) Rollout plan
- Phase 0 (canary): enable mmap-backed safetensors mapping for non-critical model family. Collect metrics for page fault rates and cold-start times.
- Phase 1 (expanded): enable shared mmap pool on multi-worker hosts, add staged upload.
- Phase 2 (GA): enable hot-swap orchestration and eviction policies by default for all hosted and dedicated nodes. Private deployment remains opt-in until full signature/keys support is validated.

Operational notes and TODOs (working-list)
- TODO: define gpu-resident-threshold per sku and expose via node labels.
- TODO: implement local mmap broker prototype (unix domain socket proof-of-concept).
- TODO: add page-fault sampling to SRE agent to correlate heavy fault rates with prefetch heuristics.
- Unresolved: canonical approach for sharing mmap across containers running as different UIDs on same host. Options: shared broker, privileged helper, or move to a sidecar. Need security review.
- Unresolved: guarantee of complete atomicity when swapping kernels that expect different tensor layouts; require model conversion pipeline to emit compatibility tags or runtime adaptors.

Backward compatibility and migration notes
- Models currently published as .pt will be supported but with a conversion recommendation. Provide a migration tool that converts .pt -> safetensors + manifest and suggest optimal loading_priority defaults.

Appendix: manifest schema (informal)
- model_id: string
- version: semver-like string
- files: list of {path, sha256, format, size_bytes}
- layers: list of {name, offset, size_bytes, dtype, quant_type, loading_priority}
- required_capabilities: list (e.g., int8-fused-kernel-v2)

References and related docs
- RFC-143: KV-cache-ejection-policy (concurrent)
- github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/mmap-broker (proto)
- internal: /confluence/serving-runtime/load-testing (perf sheets)

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally prescriptive on mmap and safetensors because we observed large wins in page-cache sharing during internal benchmarks. However, I welcome opinions on alternative approaches (e.g., zstd-chunked remote streaming) for low-memory hosts.

Contact
